questiontext.text:
Which is the best summary of the proof by contradiction above, that no quadratic is always prime?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
A good summary names the logical structure and the mechanism. Here: assume, for contradiction, that \(f(n)\) is prime for every integer \(n\); let \(p = f(1)\); the values at \(n = 1 + p\) and \(n = 1 + 2p\) are multiples of \(p\), so, being prime, all three values are \(p\); but a quadratic takes each value at most twice. So \(f(n)\) is not prime for at least one \(n\). The best summary is the third.

The other summaries fail. Trying examples can never prove the conjecture: you might miss the one counterexample. Putting \(n = c\) is the first attempt, which does not work when \(c\) or \(ac + b + 1\) is 1 or \(-1\). Expanding \(f(1 + p)\) is a correct step of the proof, but it is one step, not a summary of the whole proof.

questionvariables.text: ta1: [[g_try, false, "Try many quadratic expressions, such as \\(n^2 + 7n + 5\\), \\(n^2 - 1\\) and \\(3n^2 + 2\\), and for each one find a value of \\(n\\) that gives a number that is not prime."], [g_put, false, "Suppose \\(f(n) = an^2 + bn + c\\) and put \\(n = c\\). Then \\(f(c) = c(ac + b + 1)\\) has the two factors \\(c\\) and \\(ac + b + 1\\), so it cannot be prime."], [g_three, true, "Suppose \\(f(n)\\) is prime for every \\(n\\), and let \\(p = f(1)\\). Then \\(f(1 + p)\\) and \\(f(1 + 2p)\\) are multiples of \\(p\\), so all three values equal \\(p\\), which no quadratic can do."], [g_expand, false, "Expand \\(a(p + 1)^2 + b(p + 1) + c\\), then use \\(a + b + c = p\\) to collect the terms into the product \\((ap + 2a + b + 1)p\\), which is a multiple of \\(p\\)."]];

questionnote.text: Best summary: three values equal p

questiondescription.text: This question is based on the second attempted proof of the second conjecture (p. 53) in Section 9 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

truefeedback.text: Yes. It names the method (suppose \(f(n)\) is always prime), the key step (three values that are multiples of \(p\)) and the contradiction (a quadratic cannot take one value three times).
Trying examples is how the quest began, and it can never prove the conjecture: you might miss the one counterexample. The proof argues about every quadratic at once.
That is the first attempt, which does not work: when \(c\) or \(ac + b + 1\) is 1 or \(-1\), \(c(ac + b + 1)\) can be prime.

falsefeedback.text: That describes one step of the proof correctly, but not the whole proof: it leaves out the assumption, the third value and the contradiction.
